newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S. farm lobby wants WTO statement on agriculture.
newsitem.headline: U.S. farm lobby wants WTO statement on agriculture.

text.p: U.S. farm lobbyists called on Monday for agriculture to be included in a final declaration of targets by trade ministers gathered in Singapore ahead of negotiations on the issue in three years time.

The lobbyists also said the nearly 30 countries seeking World Trade Organization (WTO) membership, including China and Russia, should be required to make commitments on opening up their agricultural markets before joining the WTO.

"The U.S. government should place high priority on the continuation of WTO agricultural negotiations, scheduled for initiation in 1999, and hold all other WTO members to the commitment that these be comprehensive and substantive negotiations," the President's Advisory Committee for Trade Policy and Negotiations (ACTPN) said in a statement.

Farm members of the ACTPN attending the WTO meeting told journalists that agriculture, which now contributes $60 billion a year in U.S. export earnings, had to be included in the WTO's final declaration to initiate a work programme on the issue.

The ACTPN released a report on Monday containing recommendations on U.S. agricultural trade policy which urged Washington to pursue an aggressive trade policy in the sector aimed at cutting tariff and non-tariff barriers to farm trade.

The report said the 1999 WTO negotiations should seek the complete elimination, by a specified date, of all remaining market access barriers, export assistance and trade distorting measures not covered in the Uruguay round of trade talks.

"The WTO Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary (plant health) measures (SPS) complements the WTO Agreement on Agriculture and may well have the greatest impact on agricultural trade in the future," the report said.
The former agreement requires that SPS measures be based on scientific principles and permits their application only if supported by sufficient evidence of a health risk, it added.

Dean Kleckner, president of the American Farm Bureau Federation (AFBF) and a member of the ACTPN, told the news conference that market access and sanitary and phytosanitary measures should be key to China's WTO entry.

"All sorts of mischiefs can come about through phytosanitary concerns that are not really scientific. They're disguised and we certainly have to resolve that. I think they've (the Chinese) got a way to go yet prior to admittance to the WTO," he said.

China has for years refused to buy wheat from the U.S. Pacific Northwest bcause it says the grain is contaminated with the tilletia controversa kuhn (TCK) smut fungus and earlier this year cancelled shipments from the U.S. Gulf for the same reason.
Washington says the fungus is harmless and that Beijing's policy of zero tolerance is a barrier to an extra 500,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat sales a year, worth millions of dollars, to China.
In October, China banned all imports of poultry and poultry meat from 10 states in the U.S. on fears the products carried virus called highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI).

U.S. officials said at the time that there appeared to be some confusion on the part of Chinese quarantine quarantine officials over the difference between HPAI, which had not been found in the United States since 1984, and avian influenza which can be found worldwide, particularly in wild fowl.

"To prove they (the Chinese) are ready to come into the WTO not evey issue needs to be cut and dried, but it need to be much better than it is today or in my view they shouldn't come in," Kleckner said.
